blocks.title: Some Background Information:
blocks.text: How do children understand the relationship between complexity, effort, and time? As adults, we have an intuitive sense of how long a task will take to be completed, or how much effort is required, and we consider these things when planning activities and evaluating others. We are interested in investigating the roots of this capability in young children. In this study, we presented your child with pairs of pictures: each pair showed two friends with block structures in front of them. These block structures varied in the number of blocks used and/or how close they were to the block structure that was initially laid out on the table. Second, your child observed block structures that have the same number of blocks but differ in how complex they are, as well as differences between the people playing with the blocks (e.g., person with arm in a sling vs. person without sling). We are interested in evaluating if (and how) children take into account these differences when they judge which block structures are easier/harder to build. This study will allow us to understand how children consider time and effort when observing others working towards achieving various physical outcomes. If you would like to learn more about this topic, you may be interested in the following talk!

blocks.title: Compensation:
blocks.text: To thank you for your participation, we'll be emailing you a $5 Amazon gift card - this should arrive in your email inbox within the next week after we confirm your consent video and check that your child is in the age range for this study (If you don't hear from us by then, feel free to reach out!). If you participate again with another child in the age range, you'll receive one gift card per child.

blocks.title: Questions or Concerns:
blocks.text: In case of questions or concerns, please do not hesitate to contact Adani Abutto: aabutto@stanford.edu

video-config.troubleshootingIntro: If you're having any trouble or would like us to walk you through setup, please email aabutto@stanford.edu.

video-consent.datause: The researchers and study staff follow federal and state laws to protect your privacy, so all of your information and research records will be kept confidential. The only exception to these procedures for maintaining confidentiality is that we are required by law to report to the appropriate authorities suspicion of harm to your child or to others. More information on how we keep your videos and data private can be found at lookit.mit.edu/faq.
video-consent.payment: There are no costs to participating. There are also no known risks associated with this study beyond those of everyday life. Although this study will not benefit your child directly, it will add to our understanding of how children think in general. If indicated in the study description, you may be compensated for participating in this study; if this is not stated in the study description, then you will not receive any payment for your participation.
video-consent.purpose: The ability to reason about the difficulty of a task at hand is crucial to learning. For example, it helps us decide which goals to choose for ourselves and others, how to allocate our time and resources, and how to avoid unecessary failure. But how do we know how hard a given task is when we have not engaged in it before? In this study, we are interested in how children judge how easy (or hard) it is to complete different novel blockbuilding structures. The study will help us understand how children gauge task difficulty.
video-consent.PIContact: Adani Abutto (aabutto@stanford.edu) if you have any questions or inquiries about the study.
video-consent.procedures: If your child participates, on the screen, they will see pictures of different block structures, and they will be asked some questions about them. For example, your child may be asked which one of two block structures is harder/easier to build. This study has been designed to be appropriate and fun for young children.
video-consent.research_rights_statement: The Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Stanford University has approved this research study. If you have questions regarding your rights as a research subject you may contact the IRB office at 650-723-2480, or by mail at Research Compliance Office, Stanford University, 1705 El Camino Real, Palo Alto, CA 94306.

listblocks.text: For the next 10 minutes your child will see some pictures of friends playing with blocks and answer questions about them!

Please sit behind your child and allow your child to answer the questions on their own. Please don't correct your child if you disagree, or tell them they're right if you agree. We're just interested in what they think!
However, if your child doesn't know how to click yet, they can instead point to the screen, and you can click for them.
If your child gets distracted, or you need to attend to something else for a moment, you can pause the study by pressing the space bar.

If you need to end the study early, try closing the window or tab and you should see an 'exit' option pop up. You'll be prompted to note any technical problems you might be experiencing and to select a privacy level for your videos.
